This view attracted extremely harsh criticism7-9 from physicians, nu- tritionists, psychologists, and epidemiologists. Despite conflicting data on the effect of vitamin E intake on cog- nitive decline, US guidelines have suggested that vitamin E be considered in patients with Alzheimer’s disease in an attempt to slow progression of the disease. A subsequent large trial found no benefit for vitamin E over placebo (see Dementia, p.1994). A cohort study found low folate concentrations to be the predomi- nant risk factor for cognitive decline in elderly people.10 Raised homocysteine concentrations have also been found in patients with cognitive decline and dementia.11 While a 2-year controlled study found that daily homocysteine-lowering treatment with folate, vitamin B6, and vitamin B12 did not improve cognitive performance,12 another found that daily folic acid supplementa- tion for 3 years significantly improved measures of cognitive function.13 Similarly, low folate concentrations and increased homocysteine concentrations have been implicated in depression, and supple- mentation has been proposed,11 both as monotherapy, or as a means of augmenting antidepressant efficacy.14 1.
